craft_claim: A voice that repeatedly deflates without license drifts into an aggressive humor style, which carries poorer social consequences and measurably costs the speaker status.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of Research in Personality 37(1):48-75, Humor Styles Questionnaire
supporting_evidence.note: The instrument distinguishes an aggressive humor style (sarcasm, ridicule, put-downs) from affiliative humor, and relates aggressive humor use to lower psychological well-being and poorer relationships — a chronic mode with correlates, not a moment.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 112(3):431-455, eight studies
supporting_evidence.note: Humor that violates the audience's norms decreases the speaker's status; humor that fits the audience's norms (or expectations) increases it — so deflation out of key with the frame is punished.

supporting_evidence.location: Whole-book citation (open-access text read earlier in session)
supporting_evidence.note: Documented cases of failed humor show audiences noticing and sanctioning misfired mockery — the drift is legible to readers and costs credibility.

counterevidence.note: The humor-style evidence is trait-level and correlational (self-report), not a manipulation of prose register — it is adjacent evidence for the chronic-drift risk, not proof that a text's tone changes its readers.
The same literature shows norm-CONGRUENT humor raises status — the cost comes from humor out of key with the audience and frame, not from humor as such.

scope: Serial or sustained voice work where deflation repeats across passages; drift is a pattern risk, not a verdict on any single joke.
exceptions: A single sharp deflation inside a strong license (satire's chosen target, an established curmudgeon persona) need not drift; drift is defined by repetition without license or fit.
